items.title: The feeling while staying

states.label: Happy
states.sm: Sā ʻou nofo ma le fiafia.
states.note: The le-phrase after *ma* names the speaker’s state while staying.

states.label: Unhappy
states.sm: Sā ʻou nofo ma le lē fiafia.
states.note: The not-word changes the state named by the le-phrase.

items.caption: The main action stays the same. The phrase after the with-word describes the person doing it.

items.title: Ways to judge an event
items.caption: These verbs often take a le-phrase as what the sentence is about. The verb passes judgement on the event named by the phrase.

items.title: What is the whole le-phrase doing?

items.sm: Na ʻou tausi=a le pepe ma le fiafia.
items.en: I took care of the baby happily.
items.why: The phrase after *ma* names the doer’s feeling while caring for the baby.

items.sm: E lelei le putaʻafa o le puaʻa.
items.en: It is good that the pig is fat.
items.why: The judging verb calls the event named by the le-phrase good.

items.sm: E ʻese le mānaia o le ʻula.
items.why: The judging verb stresses that the quality is out of the ordinary.

items.sm: ʻO le fefe o le teine
items.en: Look how scared the girl is
items.why: The presenting particle holds up the le-phrase as an immediate comment on the girl’s reaction.

items.intro: Read the construction around the event phrase and choose its use.
